client: I’ve been spiraling about this conference presentation next week. Yesterday, I completely blanked during practice, and now I can’t stop imagining the same thing happening in front of everyone. I know you’ll probably tell me to think differently about it, but I don’t see how that helps when the fear feels so real.
therapist: I hear how real and overwhelming this fear feels for you right now, especially after that practice session. Let's explore together what was happening in that moment when you blanked—what thoughts were running through your mind at that time?

client:
I just kept thinking "Everyone can tell I'm panicking" and "I'm going to completely embarrass myself." It felt like my mind went totally blank, like all my preparation just disappeared. Even now I feel my chest getting tight just remembering it. 

I don't know if analyzing the thoughts helps though - it's not like thinking about it differently will stop it from happening again. The fear feels so physical, you know?
therapist: It makes complete sense that those thoughts would make your body react with panic—our minds and bodies are deeply connected. What if we gently explored what your body might need in those moments when the physical fear arises?

client: I guess it makes sense that my body reacts when I start panicking, but I’m not sure what it needs in those moments. It feels like everything is spinning, and I just want it to stop. When you say "explore what my body might need," I’m not even sure where to start—it feels overwhelming to think about it when I’m already so scared.
therapist: That feeling of overwhelm is completely understandable—panic can make it hard to even know where to begin. What if we started small, like noticing where you feel the tightness in your chest and simply taking one slow breath there?

client: I get what you're saying about starting small, but honestly, even focusing on my chest feels overwhelming right now. When I try to notice it, I just feel more panicked, like I’m trapped in my own body. It’s hard to believe something as simple as breathing could make a difference when everything feels so out of control.
therapist: I hear how trapped and powerless you're feeling in those moments—panic can make even small suggestions feel impossible. Would it feel safer to start by simply noticing something outside your body, like the feeling of your feet on the floor?

client: I can try that, but honestly when the panic hits, it's like my whole body goes numb. I'm not sure I'd even notice my feet on the floor when my heart is racing and my thoughts are spiraling. It just feels like everything is happening too fast to focus on small sensations.
therapist: That numbness and sense of everything moving too fast shows just how intensely your nervous system is reacting—it's trying to protect you, even if it feels overwhelming right now. What if we imagined that moment like a movie that you could pause for just one second—what might you notice in that frozen frame?

client: The idea of pausing everything sounds nice in theory, but when I try to imagine it, my brain just keeps racing anyway. It's like hitting pause on a video but the audio keeps playing in the background—I still feel that panicky undercurrent. Maybe I'm not doing it right?
therapist: I appreciate you being so honest about how this exercise feels—it's completely normal for the mind to keep racing even when we try to slow things down. What if instead of trying to stop the thoughts completely, we simply noticed them passing by, like watching cars go past a window?

client: I get what you're saying about watching thoughts pass by, but when my anxiety spikes, those thoughts feel more like speeding trucks than cars. It's hard to just observe them when they're so loud and overwhelming. I've tried mindfulness before and always end up feeling more frustrated when I can't make it work.
therapist: I hear how frustrating it's been when mindfulness feels like it's not working—those speeding truck thoughts can make any technique feel impossible in the moment. What if we shifted focus from trying to "make it work" to simply acknowledging how strong those thoughts feel right now?

client: I guess I can try just noticing how intense the thoughts feel instead of fighting them, but it still seems pointless when they're so overwhelming. Part of me worries that if I stop trying to control them, they'll just take over completely and I'll spiral.
therapist: That worry about losing control makes so much sense—it's scary to consider letting go of the fight when the thoughts feel so powerful. What if we explored what "taking over completely" would actually look like in that conference situation?

client: I guess "taking over completely" would mean that my anxiety spirals out of control and I end up panicking in the middle of the conference, maybe even having to leave. That’s my worst fear—looking weak or incapable in front of everyone. It’s hard to imagine that not happening because it feels so real when I think about it. I’m not sure how exploring that helps, though—it just makes me feel more anxious to dwell on it.
therapist: It makes complete sense that imagining that scenario would feel so frightening—your mind is trying to protect you by anticipating the worst. What if we gently explored whether there’s any evidence that this worst-case scenario has ever actually happened to you before?

client: I get what you're saying, but that's the thing - the worst case hasn't happened yet, but it feels like it could at any moment. My anxiety tells me it's just a matter of time before everything falls apart, even if it hasn't before. The uncertainty is what really gets to me.
therapist: That uncertainty can feel so threatening—your mind is trying to prepare you for danger, even when the danger isn't certain. What would it feel like to acknowledge that uncertainty while also remembering the many times you've gotten through challenging situations before?
